extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in nonlinear time series analysis (dynamical systems), e.g. physicists, neuroscientists, engineers, and applied mathematicians using recurrence plots and synchronisation analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for using recurrence plots (RPs), recurrence quantification analysis (RQA), and RP-based surrogates to detect and test phase, generalized, and lag synchronisation in coupled dynamical systems, including noise-robust parameter choices and validation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional stability approach — requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditional stability approach requires estimation of Lyapunov exponents to detect generalized synchronisation (GS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disadvantage for experimental time series: estimating Lyapunov exponents from observed data can be rather difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary system approach — requirement and limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary system approach requires an identical copy of the response system to test for GS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problematic for measured data due to noise influences and inaccuracy in system parameters; obtaining an identical copy may be infeasible in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual false nearest neighbours (MFNN) approach — suitability and limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: MFNN-based approach is suitable for analysis of experimental data but can fail when systems have more than one predominant time scale (e.g., slow and fast scales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If driver and response are not in GS but have multiple time scales, MFNN can be of order one because distances among fast-scale neighbours are of attractor size; fails for non-phase-coherent dynamics such as certain electrochemical oscillators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence-based method for GS detection — features
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrence-based method detects GS using marginal and joint probabilities of recurrence rather than distances between nearest neighbours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for experimental data with broad power spectra or multiple timescales; close in concept to transfer entropy for detecting coupling direction; computationally comparable to other approaches (distances between all pairs of points must be computed).

rubrics_metrics.name: δp,q method — extension for non-invertibility and wrinkling
rubrics_metrics.description: δp,q considers two points neighbours if they are neighbours not only at one instant but over a longer time interval, allowing detection of GS in non-invertible or wrinkled dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous extensions can be introduced in recurrence-based approaches (e.g., increasing embedding dimension) to handle such complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational demand (complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computing recurrence-based measures requires computing distances between all pairs of trajectory points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an N^2 problem; recurrence-based approach is comparable in computational demand to false nearest neighbour or δp,q approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: CP_R index — phase synchronisation detection
rubrics_metrics.description: CP_R index distinguishes oscillators in phase synchronisation (PS); transition to PS is detected when CP_R becomes of order one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice CP_R indicates onset of PS (example: PS transition at coupling µ ≈ 0.037 corresponds to CP_R ≈ 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: JP_R index — generalized and lag synchronisation detection
rubrics_metrics.description: JP_R (joint recurrence probability index) is an index for GS and lag synchronisation (LS); it indicates different regimes by plateaus and approaches one when LS is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JP_R can show multiple plateaus vs coupling strength indicating transitions; JP_R ≈ 1 signals LS (example: LS onset at µ ≈ 0.1). JP_R also fluctuates in intermittent LS regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation with Lyapunov exponents (λ2, λ4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Lyapunov spectrum to validate recurrence-based synchronisation results: λ4 becoming negative indicates onset of PS; λ2 crossing zero indicates strong amplitude correlation/LS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare CP_R and JP_R transitions to λ4 and λ2 transitions respectively to validate detection of PS and LS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction from RP — possibility and condition (ε choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under general conditions it is possible to reconstruct the underlying attractor topologically from a binary RP of a scalar time series, provided the threshold ε is chosen appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the RP one can obtain a rank-ordered time series and reconstruct the attractor via delay embedding; ε must be small enough to distinguish points but large enough to satisfy reconstruction assumptions (see next entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction algorithm assumption — max consecutive distance < ε
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithm assumes the maximum distance between two consecutive points in the rank-ordered time series is smaller than ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this assumption fails the reconstruction algorithm will not correctly recover rank order; the algorithm consists of three phases and nine steps (detailed in Appendix B.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction valid only for scalar time series (m = 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reconstruction algorithm from an RP is only valid when the RP is from a scalar time series; it does not work for RPs of m-dimensional trajectories with m > 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It remains an open question whether reconstruction is possible from RPs of higher-dimensional trajectories; first results indicate possibility only under some conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal data length for reconstruction (ε vs N)
rubrics_metrics.description: Required number of points for reliable reconstruction depends on ε and N; with uniform assumption one can estimate probability p(ε) that maximal gap < ε and therefore necessary N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using ε = 0.1 about 90 points are needed to reconstruct the time series with probability ≈ 0.999. Larger ε reduces required N but risks losing fine structures; if ε too large (e.g., 1/2 + δ in unit interval) many points become indistinguishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin surrogates (TS) — null hypothesis and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Twin surrogates are generated from RPs to create surrogates that mimic the dynamical behaviour and topological properties of the system, consistent with the null hypothesis that surrogates are independent realisations (same system, different initial conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TS are created by identifying 'twins' (points with identical RP columns) and randomly jumping to possible futures of twins to introduce randomness while preserving invariants; they are used to test if an independent process could give the same synchronisation index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin surrogate testing procedure — significance test
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate M twin surrogates and compute the synchronisation index (e.g., PS index R) between one subsystem of the original and the surrogate subsystem; compare the original index to the surrogate distribution to test the null hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reject the null at significance level α, the original R must exceed the (1 − α) quantile of the surrogate Rs (i.e., be larger than all but α·100% of Rsj). Example: generate 200 TS and compute surrogate PS indices to obtain significance levels from the empirical cumulative histogram.

rubrics_metrics.name: PS index (mean resultant length R) — definition and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: PS index R is defined as R = (1/N) |Σ_{i=1}^N e^{j ΔΦ_i}|, ranges from 0 (non-PS) to 1 (perfect PS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as synchronisation measure; large values indicate synchronisation but are not conclusive without a surrogate-based hypothesis test, especially in passive experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: normalised synchronisation measures need hypothesis testing
rubrics_metrics.description: A large normalised synchronisation index (e.g., > 0.97) alone does not provide conclusive evidence for PS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in passive experiments (cannot vary coupling), synchronisation analysis should always be accompanied by a hypothesis test using appropriate surrogates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin surrogates mimic coupling characteristics — effect on significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because twin surrogates mimic both linear and nonlinear characteristics and can share mean frequency with the original oscillator in the PS region, surrogate PS indices Rsj may be high, raising the significance limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, the empirical significance threshold increases near PS transitions; the original R must exceed this increased threshold to indicate PS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noise influence on recurrence identification — Pi,j mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational Gaussian noise maps the deterministic distance matrix Di,j to a probability Pi,j of finding a recurrence at (i,j) in the noisy RP; small noise makes P closer to a Heaviside step, larger noise smears it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical expression (Eq. 119) maps Di,j to Pi,j; even small noise reduces reliability of RP quantification (example: 4% noise can reduce recognition probability of recurrences below 0.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of errors due to observational noise
rubrics_metrics.description: Two error types: (1) false negative — a true recurrence point not recognised (probability 1 − pb) and (2) false positive — a non-recurrence point recognised as recurrence (probability 1 − pw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimise both pb and pw simultaneously by appropriate ε choice; error rates depend on noise σ and distribution of pairwise distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold ε selection relative to noise (recommended rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose threshold ε at least five times the standard deviation of observational noise, ε ≳ 5 σ (higher-dimensional systems may require ε > 5 σ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice minimises errors from noise for a wide class of processes; if ε is smaller the noise will dominate detection of recurrence points; if ε is too large fine structures are lost; if ε ≈ std of underlying process recurrence density becomes too high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of ε on RP statistics (diagonal line distributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper ε (e.g., ε = σ) biases RP statistics such as cumulative distribution of diagonal lines in presence of noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: logistic map contaminated with Gaussian white noise — choose ε = 5σ to recover diagonal line distribution consistent with noise-free case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimation of noise level via dynamical invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: Use relationships between dynamical invariants and noise/threshold (e.g., correlation entropy K2(ε)) to estimate observational noise level σ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit analytical function K2(ε) to entropy computed from RPs to infer σ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unstable periodic orbit (UPO) localisation via RP
rubrics_metrics.description: UPOs appear as 'periodic' windows in RPs: uninterrupted equally spaced diagonal lines correspond to periodic motion and indicate presence of UPOs; periods estimated from vertical distances multiplied by sampling time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify windows with periodic patterns; estimate period via vertical distance between recurrence points or mean length of white vertical lines; limitations include finite-length trajectories not visiting all UPOs and RPs being less appropriate for high-period or very unstable UPOs.
